findings.text: Paravirtual feature selectors are small integers: clocksource second generation is 3, async page fault is 4, steal time is 5, paravirtual end of interrupt is 6, paravirtual unhalt is 7, paravirtual TLB flush is 9, async fault delivered as exit is 10, send IPI is 11, poll control is 12, sched yield is 13, async fault as interrupt is 14, MSI extended destination is 15, map GPA range is 16, migration control is 17, realtime hints is 0, and clocksource stable indicator is bit 24.

Legacy paravirtual clocks live at model specific register numbers 0x11 for wall clock and 0x12 for system time, with enable indicated by value 1. New range uses base 0x4B564D00 through 0x4B564D08 in order for wall clock, system time, async fault enable, steal time, end of interrupt enable, poll control, async fault interrupt vector, async fault acknowledge, and migration control.

Steal time area begins with a 64 bit cumulative steal counter, then 32 bit version and 32 bit flags, then an 8 bit preempted indicator plus three reserved bytes, then eleven 32 bit pad words. Consumer is expected to sample version around reads to detect concurrent update.

Steal area requires 32 byte alignment expressed as alignment shift 5, with valid address bits above that shift and low reserved mask covering the alignment bits shifted by one. Guest preempted state is bit 0 and request to flush TLB is bit 1 of the associated flag byte.
Clock pairing record holds signed 64 bit seconds and nanoseconds, an unsigned 64 bit time stamp counter value, a 32 bit flags word, and nine 32 bit pad words. Flag value 0 selects wallclock pairing.

Async page fault control uses bit 0 for enabled, bit 1 for send always, bit 2 for delivery as fault exit, bit 3 for delivery as interrupt, with low 8 bits holding the interrupt vector. Batched MMU operations are capped at 32 entries. Migration ready is indicated by bit 0.
Map GPA range page size selector uses 0 for 4K, bit 0 for 2M, and bit 1 for 1G. Encryption state is encoded in bits starting at shift 4, with 0 meaning decrypted and 1 meaning encrypted.

Paravirtual MMU operations are numbered 1 for write entry, 2 for flush TLB, and 3 for release page table. Page ready protocol uses reason 1 for not present and 2 for ready. End of interrupt uses bit 0, where mask value 1 means enabled and 0 means disabled.

Each MMU operation starts with a header carrying a 32 bit opcode plus 32 bit pad. Write entry appends physical address of entry and new value as two 64 bit fields. Flush carries only the header. Release appends a 64 bit page table physical address. Async fault vcpu data holds 32 bit flags for not-present delivery via fault, 32 bit token for ready delivery via interrupt, and 56 pad bytes.
Perf decoding reserves 20 characters for decoded strings. The vcpu key is vcpu_id, entry trace is kvm:kvm_entry, exit trace is kvm:kvm_exit, and reason key is exit_reason.
Local descriptor table supports 8192 entries of 8 bytes each. Segment contents codes are 0 for data, 1 for stack, and 2 for code.

User descriptor carries entry number, base address, and limit as 32 bit values, then single bit flags for 32 bit segment, two bit contents, read or execute only, limit in pages, not present, and usable. On 64 bit builds an extra long mode bit exists.
When a descriptor originates from a 32 bit program the kernel must act as if the long mode bit is clear regardless of the stored value, because 32 bit callers may leave that bit uninitialized.

Machine check record starts with six 64 bit fields for status, miscellaneous, address, global status, instruction pointer, and time stamp counter, then 64 bit wall time, then vendor, inject flags, severity and pad as bytes, 32 bit cpuid, bytes for code segment, bank, cpu number and finished, 32 bit extended cpu, socket and apic identifiers, three 64 bit capability and SMCA fields, 64 bit inventory number, 32 bit microcode revision, and 64 bit kernel flags.
Machine check device exposes three read ioctls on type M with numbers 1, 2, and 3 returning integer lengths or flags for record length, log length, and get-clear flags.
Memory map hints add 0x40 to restrict allocation to 32 bit addresses and 0x80 to require mapping above 4G.

64 bit message queue descriptor holds permission substructure, three signed long timestamps for send, receive and change, three unsigned long counters for bytes, message count and queue byte limit, two pid values for last sender and receiver, and two unsigned long unused words.
MSR device exposes read and write register ioctls on type c with numbers 0xA0 and 0xA1, each transferring eight 32 bit values.

Memory type range entries appear in two layouts. Legacy layout uses native long base with 32 bit size and type, and get entry adds register number first. Fixed width layout uses 64 bit base, 32 bit size and type, with get entry ordering base, size, register number, type and pad. Variable range register image holds four 32 bit halves for base low and high and mask low and high. Range type is an 8 bit value.

Fixed range count is 88 and variable range maximum is 256. Variable range base and mask register numbers derive from index as 0x200 plus twice index for base and plus one for mask. Ioctl family uses type M.

Memory type range control exposes ten ioctls numbered 0 through 9 for add, set, delete, get, kill and page-granular variants, where get operations are bidirectional and the others carry user data into the kernel.
Cacheability types are 0 uncacheable, 1 write combining, 4 writethrough, 5 write protected, 6 writeback, with 7 as count of types and 0xFF as invalid marker.

Perf register identifiers order general registers AX through GS then R8 through R15, with 32 bit maximum after GS and 64 bit maximum after R15. Extended vector registers XMM0 through XMM15 occupy even positions from 32 upward stepping by two to cover 128 bit width, with overall extended maximum after XMM15. Extended mask covers all bits from XMM0 upward.

32 bit compatibility defines mode, ipc pid, uid, gid, and old device as 16 bit unsigned. 64 bit defines old uid and gid as 16 bit unsigned and old device as unsigned long. X32 defines signed and unsigned long as 64 bit long long.

x86 process control numbers use 0x1001 to 0x1004 for set GS, set FS, get FS, and get GS; 0x1011 and 0x1012 for get and set CPUID faulting; 0x1021 through 0x1025 for extended state component support, permission query and request including guest permission; 0x2001 to 0x2003 for mapping VDSO for X32, 32 bit, and 64 bit; 0x4001 to 0x4004 for untag mask, tagged address enable, max tag bits, and forced tagged SVA; and 0x5001 to 0x5005 for shadow stack enable, disable, lock, unlock, and status. Tile config component is 17 and tile data is 18.
Shadow stack feature word uses bit 0 for shadow stack itself and bit 1 for write to shadow stack.

Flag bit positions are carry 0, fixed always-on 1, parity 2, auxiliary 4, zero 6, sign 7, trap 8, interrupt 9, direction 10, overflow 11, privilege level start 12 covering two bits, nested task 14, resume 16, virtual mode 17, alignment check 18, virtual interrupt 19, virtual pending 20, and CPUID detection 21.

Control register zero enables are protection 0, monitor coprocessor 1, emulation 2, task switched 3, extension type 4, numeric error 5, write protect 16, alignment mask 18, not writethrough 29, cache disable 30, and paging 31.

Control register three carries writethrough bit 3, cache disable bit 4, 12 bit process context identifier in low bits, linear masking for user at bits 61 and 62 for different widths, and no-flush preservation at bit 63.

Several encodings carry width rules: privilege level occupies two bits, process identifier occupies twelve low bits with all-ones mask, extended vector registers each consume two identifier bits, variable range register numbers advance by two per index, steal base must satisfy 32 byte alignment, and flag bit 1 is defined as always set.

Compatibility hazards include long mode bit possibly uninitialized from 32 bit callers so it must be ignored there, legacy cpu number field superseded by extended cpu identifier, synd and instance identifier valid only on SMCA systems, and reserved pad and mask bits that must not be interpreted as data.

This dossier exposes userspace control interfaces for KVM paravirtual clocks and async faults via feature bits and MSR numbers, machine check records via ioctls, MTRR entries via ioctls, MSR access via ioctls, LDT descriptors, message queue descriptors, perf register identifiers, and x86 process controls.
